blocks.p: So each commander received his authority from the King’s hand; the day was appointed and the meeting place fixed, and each appeared in such splendor as suited his cause and calling. Then, after a fresh entertainment from Shaddai, they set out with flying colors to march toward the famous town of Mansoul. Captain Boanerges led the vanguard, Captain Conviction and Captain Judgment made up the main body, and Captain Execution brought up the rear. They had a long way to go (for the town of Mansoul was far from the court of Shaddai), and they marched through the regions and countries of many peoples, harming and abusing no one, but blessing wherever they came. And all along the way they lived at the King’s expense.

After traveling like this for many days, at last they came within sight of Mansoul; and when they saw it, the captains could not for their lives help mourning a while over the town, for they quickly saw how it lay prostrate under the will, ways, and designs of Diabolus.

Well, to be brief, the captains came up before the town, marched up to Ear-gate, and sat down there, for that was the place of hearing. And when they had pitched their tents and dug their trenches, they set themselves to make their assault.

Now at first the townsfolk, seeing so gallant a company, so splendidly equipped and so excellently disciplined, with their glittering armor and their flying colors, could not help coming out of their houses to gaze. But that cunning fox Diabolus, afraid that after such a sight the people might, at a sudden summons, open the gates to the captains, came down from the castle in all haste and made them withdraw into the heart of the town, and there made them this lying and deceitful speech:

“Gentlemen,” he said, “although you are my trusty and well-beloved friends, I cannot help scolding you a little for your careless act just now, in going out to gaze at that great and mighty force that sat down before us only yesterday, and has now dug in to lay siege to the famous town of Mansoul. Do you know who they are, where they come from, and what they mean by sitting down before us? They are the ones I told you about long ago, who would come to destroy this town, and against whom I have gone to the expense of arming your bodies from head to foot, besides building great fortifications for your minds. Why, then, did you not rather, at their very first appearance, cry out, ‘Light the beacons!’ and raise the alarm through the whole town, so that we might all have been in a posture of defense, ready to receive them with the highest acts of defiance? Then you would have shown yourselves men after my own heart; whereas by what you have done you have made me half afraid (I say, half afraid) that when it comes to push of pike between them and us, I shall find you lack the courage to hold out. Why have I commanded a watch, and ordered you to double your guards at the gates? Why have I labored to make you as hard as iron, and your hearts like the lower millstone? Was it, do you think, so that you might show yourselves women, and go out like a flock of innocents to gaze at your mortal enemies? For shame, for shame! Put yourselves in a posture of defense, beat the drum, gather together in warlike order, so that our enemies may know that before they conquer this town there are valiant men in Mansoul.

“I will scold and rebuke you no further; but I charge you, let me see no more such actions. From now on, let no man of you, without orders from me, so much as show his head over the wall of Mansoul. You have heard me now. Do as I have commanded, and you will make it possible for me to dwell securely with you, and to take care of your safety and honor as well as my own. Farewell.”

Now the townsmen were strangely changed. They were like men struck with panic; they ran to and fro through the streets of the town of Mansoul, crying out, “Help, help! The men who have turned the world upside down have come here too!” [Acts 17:6] Nor could any of them be quiet after that; but like men out of their wits they kept crying, “The destroyers of our peace and our people have come!”

This went down well with Diabolus. “Ah,” he said to himself, “I like this well. Now it is as I would have it; now you show your obedience to your prince. Only hold to this, and then let them take the town if they can.”

Well, before the King’s forces had sat before Mansoul three days, Captain Boanerges commanded his trumpeter to go down to Ear-gate and there, in the name of the great Shaddai, summon Mansoul to hear the message he had been commanded to deliver in his Master’s name. So the trumpeter, whose name was Take-heed-what-you-hear, went up to Ear-gate as he was commanded, and there sounded his trumpet for a hearing. But no one appeared to answer or pay any heed, for Diabolus had commanded it so. So the trumpeter returned and told his captain how he had fared; and the captain was grieved, but told him to go to his tent.
Again Captain Boanerges sent his trumpeter to Ear-gate to sound for a hearing as before; but again they kept close and gave him no answer, so obedient were they to the command of Diabolus their king.

Then the captains and the other field officers called a council of war to consider what more should be done to win Mansoul. After close and thorough debate on the contents of their commissions, they decided to give the town yet another summons to hear, by the hand of the trumpeter already named. But if that was refused, they said, and the town still held out, then they were resolved (and told the trumpeter to say so) to compel them by whatever means they could to the obedience of their King.

So Captain Boanerges commanded his trumpeter to go up to Ear-gate again and, in the name of the great King Shaddai, give it a very loud summons to come down without delay to Ear-gate, there to give a hearing to the King’s most noble captains. So the trumpeter went up to Ear-gate as he was commanded, sounded his trumpet, and gave Mansoul a third summons. He said, moreover, that if they still refused, the captains of his prince would come down on them in strength and try to bring them to obedience by force.

Then my Lord Willbewill stood up. He was the governor of the town (this Willbewill was the apostate mentioned before) and the keeper of the gates of Mansoul. With big and blustering words he demanded of the trumpeter who he was, where he came from, and why he was making such a hideous noise at the gate and speaking such intolerable words against the town of Mansoul.

The trumpeter answered, “I am the servant of the most noble captain, Captain Boanerges, general of the forces of the great King Shaddai, against whom you yourself and the whole town of Mansoul have rebelled and lifted up the heel. My master the captain has a special message for this town, and for you as a member of it. If you will hear it peaceably, well and good; if not, you must take what follows.”
“I will carry your words to my lord,” said the Lord Willbewill, “and find out what he will say.”

But the trumpeter replied at once, “Our message is not to the giant Diabolus, but to the miserable town of Mansoul; and we will pay no regard at all to any answer he makes, or anyone makes for him. We are sent to this town to recover it from under his cruel tyranny, and to persuade it to submit, as it did in former times, to the most excellent King Shaddai.”
“I will take your errand to the town,” said the Lord Willbewill.

“Sir,” the trumpeter replied, “do not deceive us, or in doing so you will deceive yourselves far more. For we are resolved, if you do not submit peaceably, to make war on you and bring you under by force. And as a sign of the truth of what I say, tomorrow you will see the black flag with its hot, burning thunderbolts set up on the mount, as a token of defiance against your prince, and of our resolve to bring you back to your Lord and rightful King.”

So the Lord Willbewill came down from the wall, and the trumpeter went back to the camp, where the captains and officers of the mighty King Shaddai gathered to learn whether he had obtained a hearing, and what had come of his errand. So the trumpeter told them.

“When I had sounded my trumpet and called aloud to the town for a hearing, my Lord Willbewill, the governor of the town, who has charge of the gates, came up, and looking over the wall asked me who I was, where I came from, and why I was making this noise. So I told him my errand, and by whose authority I brought it. ‘Then,’ he said, ‘I will tell it to the governor and to Mansoul.’ And then I came back to my lords.”
Then the brave Boanerges said, “Let us lie still in our trenches a while yet, and see what these rebels will do.”

Now when the time drew near that Mansoul must give audience to the brave Boanerges and his companions, orders went out that every man of war in the camp of Shaddai should stand to arms as one man and be ready: if Mansoul would hear, to receive it to mercy at once; but if not, to force it into subjection. So when the day came, the trumpets sounded through the whole camp, to have the men of war ready for the work of the day. But when those in Mansoul heard the trumpets sounding through the camp of Shaddai, they could think of nothing but an assault on the town, and at first they were thrown into great dismay. But after they had settled a little, they too made what preparation they could for war, in case the assault came, or at least to secure themselves.
When the last moment had come, Boanerges was determined to hear their answer, and sent out his trumpeter again to summon Mansoul to a hearing of the message they had brought from Shaddai.

So he went and sounded, and the townsmen came up, but made Ear-gate as fast as they could. When they had come up to the top of the wall, Captain Boanerges asked to see the Lord Mayor. But my Lord Incredulity was Lord Mayor now, for he had come in in place of my Lord Lustings. So Incredulity came up and showed himself over the wall. But when Captain Boanerges set eyes on him, he cried out aloud, “This is not he! Where is my Lord Understanding, the ancient Lord Mayor of the town of Mansoul? It is to him that I would deliver my message.”

Then the giant (for Diabolus had come down too) said to the captain, “Mr. Captain, by your boldness you have given Mansoul at least four summonses to submit to your King, by whose authority I do not know, nor will I dispute it now. I ask you, then, what is the reason for all this fuss? What would you be at, if you even knew yourselves?”

Then Captain Boanerges, whose were the black colors and whose escutcheon was the three burning thunderbolts, took no notice of the giant or his speech, but addressed himself to the town of Mansoul. “Know this, O unhappy and rebellious Mansoul: the most gracious King, the great King Shaddai, my Master, has sent me to you with a commission” (and here he showed the town his broad seal) “to bring you back to his obedience. He has commanded me, if you yield to my summons, to deal with you as if you were my friends or brothers; but he has also ordered that if, after summons to submit, you still hold out and rebel, we should try to take you by force.”

Then Captain Conviction stood forth (his were the pale colors, and for an escutcheon he had the book of the law wide open, with its flame of fire) and said, “Hear, O Mansoul! You, O Mansoul, were once famous for innocence, but now you have sunk into lies and deceit. You have heard what my brother, Captain Boanerges, has said; and it is your wisdom, and will be your happiness, to bow and accept terms of peace and mercy when they are offered, especially by one against whom you have rebelled, and who has power to tear you in pieces; for so has Shaddai our King, and when he is angry, nothing can stand before him. If you say you have not sinned, or rebelled against our King, the whole of your conduct since the day you cast off his service (and that was the beginning of your sin) will testify against you well enough. What else does it mean, your listening to the tyrant and receiving him as your king? What else does it mean, your rejecting the laws of Shaddai and obeying Diabolus? Yes, and what does it mean, your taking up arms against us, the faithful servants of your King, and shutting your gates on us? Be ruled, then, and accept my brother’s invitation. Do not let the time of mercy slip past, but ‘come to terms quickly with your adversary.’ [Matt. 5:25] Ah, Mansoul! do not let yourself be kept from mercy, and run into a thousand miseries, by the flattering wiles of Diabolus. Perhaps that piece of deceit will try to make you believe that we are seeking our own profit in this service of ours; but know that it is obedience to our King, and love for your happiness, that has moved us to undertake it.

“Again I say to you, O Mansoul, consider whether it is not amazing grace that Shaddai should humble himself as he does. Now, by us, he reasons with you by way of entreaty and sweet persuasion, that you would submit yourselves to him. Does he have the need of you that we are sure you have of him? No, no; but he is merciful, and does not want Mansoul to die, but to turn to him and live.”

Then Captain Judgment stood forth, whose were the red colors, and who had the burning fiery furnace for his escutcheon, and he said, “You inhabitants of the town of Mansoul, who have lived so long in rebellion and acts of treason against the King Shaddai, know that we do not come to this place today, in this manner, with our message out of our own heads, or to avenge a quarrel of our own. It is the King my Master who has sent us to bring you back to obedience to him; and if you refuse to yield peaceably, we have a commission to compel you. And never think, nor let the tyrant Diabolus persuade you to think, that our King is not able by his power to bring you down and lay you under his feet; for ‘he is the Maker of all things’ [Jer. 10:16], and if he touches the mountains, they smoke. Nor will the gate of the King’s mercy stand open forever; for the day ‘that shall burn like an oven’ [Mal. 4:1] is before him. Yes, it ‘hastens greatly’ [Zeph. 1:14]; it does not slumber.

“O Mansoul, is it a small thing in your eyes that our King offers you mercy, and that after so many provocations? Yes, he still holds out his golden scepter to you, and will not yet allow his gate to be shut against you. Will you provoke him to do it? If so, consider what I say: it will be opened to you no more forever. ‘Though you say you do not see him, yet judgment is before him; therefore trust in him.’ [Job 35:14] Yes, ‘because there is wrath, beware lest he take you away with his stroke; then a great ransom cannot deliver you. Will he value your riches? No, not gold, nor all the forces of strength.’ [Job 36:18-19] ‘He has prepared his throne for judgment’ [Ps. 9:7]; for ‘he will come with fire, and with his chariots like a whirlwind, to render his anger with fury, and his rebuke with flames of fire.’ [Isa. 66:15] Therefore, O Mansoul, take heed lest, when you have ‘fulfilled the judgment of the wicked,’ justice and judgment ‘take hold of you.’” [Job 36:17]

Now while Captain Judgment was making this speech to the town of Mansoul, some observed that Diabolus trembled. But the captain went on with his discourse. “O woeful town of Mansoul, will you not even yet open your gate to receive us, the deputies of your King, who would rejoice to see you live? ‘Can your heart endure, or can your hands be strong,’ in the day when he deals with you in judgment? [Ezek. 22:14] I say, can you endure to be forced to drink, as one would drink sweet wine, the sea of wrath that our King has prepared for Diabolus and his angels? Consider, consider in time.”

Then the fourth captain, the noble Captain Execution, stood forth and said, “O town of Mansoul, once famous but now like the fruitless bough, once the delight of the high ones but now a den for Diabolus, listen to me also, and to the words that I shall speak to you in the name of the great Shaddai. ‘Look, the axe is laid to the root of the trees; every tree, therefore, that does not bear good fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.’ [Matt. 3:10]

“You, O town of Mansoul, have until now been this fruitless tree. You bear nothing but thorns and briers. Your evil fruit shows that you are not a good tree; ‘your grapes are grapes of gall, your clusters are bitter.’ [Deut. 32:32] You have rebelled against your King; and look, we, the power and force of Shaddai, are the axe that is laid to your root. What do you say? Will you turn? I say again, tell me before the first blow is struck: will you turn? Our axe must first be laid to your root before it is laid at your root. It must first be laid to your root by way of threatening, before it is laid at your root by way of execution; and between the two, your repentance is required, and that is all the time you have. What will you do? Will you turn, or shall I strike? If I fetch my blow, Mansoul, down you go; for I have a commission to lay my axe at your roots as well as to them, and nothing but yielding to our King will prevent the execution. What are you fit for, O Mansoul, if mercy does not prevent it, but to be cut down and thrown into the fire and burned?

“O Mansoul, patience and forbearance do not go on forever. A year, or two, or three, they may; but if you provoke them by three years’ rebellion (and you have already done more than that), what follows but ‘Cut it down’? No, ‘after that you shall cut it down.’ [Luke 13:7-9] And do you think these are only threats, or that our King has no power to carry out his words? O Mansoul, you will find that in the words of our King, when sinners make little or light of them, there is not only threatening, but burning coals of fire.

“You have been a tree that only uses up the ground for a long time already; will you go on so still? Your sin has brought this army to your walls; and shall it bring it in, in judgment, to do execution in your town? You have heard what the captains have said, and still you shut your gates. Speak out, Mansoul: will you go on so, or will you accept terms of peace?”

These brave speeches of the four noble captains the town of Mansoul refused to hear; yet the sound of them beat against Ear-gate, though their force could not break it open. In the end the town asked for time to prepare its answer to these demands. The captains then told them that if they would throw out to them one Mr. Dwell-on-it who was in the town, so that they might reward him according to his works, they would give them time to consider; but if they would not throw him over the wall, they would give them none.
“For,” they said, “we know that as long as Dwell-on-it draws breath in Mansoul, all sound consideration will be thrown into confusion, and nothing but mischief will come of it.”

Then Diabolus, who was there, unwilling to lose his Dwell-on-it because he was his orator (and lose him he certainly would have, could the captains have laid their fingers on him), resolved at that moment to give them an answer himself. But then, changing his mind, he commanded the Lord Mayor of the day, the Lord Incredulity, to do it. “My lord,” he said, “give these renegades an answer, and speak out, so that Mansoul may hear and understand you.”

So Incredulity, at Diabolus’s command, began. “Gentlemen,” he said, “you have camped here against Mansoul, as we see, to the disturbance of our prince and the harassment of the town. But where you come from we will not know, and what you are we will not believe. You tell us, indeed, in your terrible speech, that you have this authority from Shaddai; but by what right he commands you to do it, of that we shall remain ignorant.

“You have also, by that same authority, summoned this town to desert her lord and, for protection, to yield herself up to the great Shaddai your King, flatteringly telling her that if she does, he will pass over her past offenses and not charge her with them.
“Further, to the terror of Mansoul, you have threatened great and grievous destruction to punish her if she does not consent to do as you would have her.

“Now, captains, wherever you come from, and however right your designs may be, know that neither my Lord Diabolus, nor I, his servant Incredulity, nor yet our brave Mansoul, cares anything for your persons, your message, or the King who you say has sent you. His power, his greatness, his vengeance, we do not fear; nor will we yield at all to your summons.

“As for the war you threaten to make on us, we must defend ourselves in it as well as we can; and know that we are not without the means to defy you. In short (for I will not be tedious), I tell you that we take you for some vagabond, renegade crew, who have shaken off all obedience to your King, banded together in a riotous mob, and are roving from place to place to see whether, by the flatteries you are so skilled at on the one hand and the threats you think will frighten on the other, you can make some foolish town, city, or country desert its place and leave it to you. But Mansoul is none of them.

“To conclude: we do not dread you, we do not fear you, nor will we obey your summons. Our gates we will shut against you, and our place we will keep you out of. Nor will we put up for long with your sitting down before us like this. Our people must live in quiet, and your presence disturbs them. So pack up, bag and baggage, and be gone, or we will let fly at you from the walls.”

This speech of old Incredulity’s was seconded by desperate Willbewill, in words to this effect: “Gentlemen, we have heard your demands and the noise of your threats, and we have heard the sound of your summons; but we do not fear your force, we do not regard your threats, and we will remain just as you found us. And we command you to be gone from these parts within three days, or you shall know what it is to dare to rouse the lion Diabolus when he is asleep in his town of Mansoul.”

The Recorder, whose name was Forget-Good, added this as well: “Gentlemen, my lords, as you see, have answered your rough and angry speeches with mild and gentle words. They have, moreover, in my hearing, given you leave to depart quietly as you came. So take their kindness and be gone. We might have come out against you in force and made you feel the edge of our swords; but as we love ease and quiet ourselves, so we do not love to hurt or trouble others.”
Then the town of Mansoul shouted for joy, as if Diabolus and his crew had won some great advantage over the captains. They rang the bells, made merry, and danced upon the walls.

Diabolus went back to the castle, and the Lord Mayor and the Recorder to their places; but the Lord Willbewill took special care that the gates should be secured with double guards, double bolts, and double locks and bars, and that Ear-gate especially should be the better watched, for that was the gate by which the King’s forces most sought to enter. The Lord Willbewill made one old Mr. Prejudice, an angry and ill-natured fellow, captain of the guard at that gate, and put under his command sixty men called deaf men: men well suited to that service, since they paid no heed to the words of the captains or of the soldiers.
